errors.description: The photograph is framed a little wider than the tech-pack crop, taking in the shirt collar at the top and a band of trouser at the bottom.
errors.expected: The drawing is cropped from mid-chest to the pointed hem.
errors.actual: The render runs from the collar to just below the hem points, so the placket occupies a slightly smaller share of the frame than a mid-chest crop would give.
errors.correction: None required - this option is defined by which of the two front panels laps over the other, so both front edges and the whole closure line have to stay in frame; the slightly wider crop is what makes that readable, and the closure still runs the full height of the picture.

lockedFeatures: reverse (right-over-left) fastening: frame-LEFT panel on top, buttonholes worked into it, pressed front edge running down immediately to the right of the buttonhole row, frame-RIGHT panel underneath with its buttons hidden
no buttonhole and no button anywhere in the right half of the picture

notes: Attempt 3 finally renders the drawn reverse fastening. The pressed front edge is a single clean vertical line and every worked buttonhole sits to its LEFT, exactly as the tech pack draws it - the frame-left panel (the wearer's RIGHT front) laps over, and the right half of the picture is unbroken cloth with no buttonholes and no visible buttons. The necktie fix from attempt 2 is retained, so the closure reads uninterrupted from the V-neck to the hem points. Lower welt pockets, double-pointed hem, cloth, background and absence of annotation all match. What unlocked it was naming the concept ('the way a woman's garment fastens') alongside a purely pixel-space instruction ('every buttonhole in the LEFT half of the picture'); two earlier attempts phrased in wearer-side tailoring terms both reverted to the conventional menswear closure.
